problems.description: Single flat module taskapp.py duplicates an app-factory + SQLite pattern that already exists in the worktree (app.py, repositories.py) instead of extending the existing layered structure; all routes and DB access live in one 140-line file with no repository/package boundary.

Every route repeats the same open-connection/try-finally/close boilerplate; no shared connection context (e.g. flask.g or a repository helper), which is the main driver of the +2 smells and +25 cognitive complexity delta.
update_task re-fetches the row then validates and updates in one nested handler, concentrating the majority of the +25 cognitive complexity in a single function.
No DELETE endpoint for a task management API, so the resource lifecycle is incomplete and has no test coverage.

The 0.73 convention score is driven by violations in pre-existing files not touched by this diff (app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py); only taskapp.py is in the commit and its listed violation ('Classes should use PascalCase') contradicts the diff, which defines no classes.
Route handlers and task_id parameters lack type hints, inconsistent with the typed helpers (get_db/init_db) in the same module.
Measurement reports 9 convention violations but lists only 8; count mismatch is a discrepancy between measurement and listing.

strengths: Parameterized SQL throughout (parameter injection safe), bugs +0, duplications 0.0%
App-factory pattern with DATABASE config and tmp_path-based test fixture giving isolated, runnable tests
Comprehensive test suite covering happy paths, validation errors (400), and missing-resource 404s
Consistent JSON error handling via 404/405 error handlers and input validation
UTC timestamps and connection cleanup via try/finally
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested greenfield CRUD API (parameterized SQL, app factory, zero bugs) that is net-positive but sits in a flat single file rather than the codebase's existing layered structure, and whose 0.73 convention score is inflated by pre-existing violations outside this commit — including a taskapp.py PascalCase flag that contradicts the actual code.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded dev value when the env var is unset; if deployed without configuration, JWTs are forgeable. The name is a loud warning but there is no guard to fail closed in production.

No tests added for the new auth surface (register/login, token expiry, ownership isolation, 401/400/409 paths) in a feature_addition session; the diff is +320 lines of security-critical logic with zero test coverage.
No password strength/length validation and no rate limiting on /auth/login; brute-force protection is absent.
Cognitive complexity increased +31 per SonarQube, concentrated in the nested make_token/require_auth closures inside create_app, which inflates the single-file module toward monolith territory.
register() does a SELECT-then-INSERT without catching sqlite3.IntegrityError, so a username race between the check and insert surfaces as a 500 instead of a 409.
Adds PyJWT as a new import (part of the +4 imports); no requirements/environment update is included in this commit, so a fresh checkout of the session may fail to run.

Measured convention score 0.73 with 9 violations, but 8 of 9 are in pre-existing files (app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py) and the remaining taskapp.py one ('Classes should use PascalCase') is not introduced by this diff — no new classes are added here.

strengths: Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than stored in plaintext.
JWT includes exp and both ExpiredSignatureError and InvalidTokenError are handled with distinct 401 responses.
Tasks are scoped to the authenticated user (owner_id filter on list/get), giving real per-user data isolation.
Backward-compatible migration via PRAGMA table_info() adds owner_id to pre-existing databases without data loss.
Uses functools.wraps, request.get_json(silent=True), correct 400/401/409 status codes, and consistent conn.close() in finally blocks.
Stays within the existing single-file Flask architecture (nested db()/helpers, init_db migration style, jsonify error handlers).
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, security-conscious JWT auth feature that respects the existing single-file Flask architecture and adds proper owner-scoping plus a backward-compatible schema migration, but ships without tests and with a risky hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback that counts as technical debt.

problems.description: DISCREPANCY: the measured convention violations flag app.py and repositories.py, which are not touched by this commit — the scan appears to cover the whole worktree, not this diff. Only celery_config.py/notifications.py/taskapp.py are actually in scope.

DISCREPANCY: 'broker_url'/'result_backend' and 'celery_app'/'logger' flagged as UPPER_CASE violations are false positives — Celery config keys and app-instance handles are conventionally lowercase by design.

Transition detection reads previous_status immediately after status from the same pre-update row; correctness depends on status being reassigned to the new value later in the handler. Implicit and fragile — reflected in the +13 cognitive complexity delta.
Fallback of f"{username}@example.com" fabricates emails for users who don't supply one, so notifications get enqueued to non-existent addresses.
Error path (broker down / .delay() raising) is caught but untested; tests only cover the happy path via mocked delay.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: celery_config.py (config), notifications.py (app+tasks), taskapp.py (consumer) — matches the story's integration arc.
Schema migration via PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE adds email to pre-existing DBs without touching existing rows.
Transition-gated trigger (only fires on pending->completed) plus six edge-case tests covering non-completed, title-only, create, and already-completed updates.
Notification enqueue wrapped in try/except so a Celery failure never breaks the request response.
Correct operational choice: defaults to redis://localhost:6379, the dedicated story-app Redis, per framework isolation rules.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound, well-tested async-notification integration whose 0.73 convention score is deflated by linter false positives on Celery's required-lowercase config keys and pre-existing files outside this diff, with only minor debt from a fragile status-transition pattern and fabricated fallback emails.

problems.description: Inconsistent connection handling: create_table takes a conn parameter while all other BaseRepository methods open their own connection via _connect(); init_db instantiates UserRepository/TaskRepository merely to call create_table(conn). This dual pattern is a small API-design smell; create_table could be a @staticmethod/@classmethod taking only conn.

TaskRepository.update() updates a task by id without owner_id scoping, breaking the authorization pattern established by get_for_owner/list_for_owner. If any route calls update() directly, the ownership check is silently bypassed — worth confirming taskapp.py still enforces it.

Connection-per-call pattern: every method opens, uses, and closes its own SQLite connection with duplicated try/finally boilerplate. Acceptable for this app size, but a shared session/context-manager would remove repetition.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: taskapp.py no longer touches sqlite3 directly; all persistence lives in a dedicated repository layer with a coherent BaseRepository ABC contract.
Meaningful DRY reduction: get_by_id/delete/list_all are factored into the base class, netting -142 lines while adding 1 function and 3 classes.
Zero regression per SonarQube: +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0 cognitive complexity, +0 duplications.
Migration logic (ALTER TABLE for new email/owner_id columns) was preserved verbatim, so pre-existing databases continue to work.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, convention-compliant repository-layer extraction that respects existing patterns and preserves schema migrations; the 0.73 convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py), not by this commit, though its new code could tighten connection handling and owner-scoping in TaskRepository.update().

problems.description: Limiter key_prefix=f"taskapp:{uuid4().hex}" is unique per app instance, so rate-limit counters reset on every restart and multiply across worker processes, defeating the redis-backed distributed limit implied by RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI. Use a stable env-derived prefix and scope per-instance randomness to tests only.
list_tasks() grew inline cursor/limit parsing and validation, adding cognitive complexity (+39 measured) and 2 smells; extracting a parse/validate helper would keep the endpoint flat.
count_for_owner() runs a COUNT(*) scan on every list page even when only pagination is needed, and 'total' can drift under concurrent writes; acceptable at this scale but worth flagging.
The rate_limited_client fixture is added but the visible diff shows no test actually asserting the 429 response / error handler path it exists to exercise.

strengths: Cursor/keyset pagination with limit+1 has-more detection avoids offset scans and stays stable under inserts, with a separate COUNT preserved for total
Rate limits are keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback, which is auth-aware rather than naive IP limiting
Follows existing DI and repository patterns: new params threaded through create_app with env fallbacks, constants extracted as UPPER_CASE, integer/range validation returns proper 400s
Response-shape change is covered by updated tests and a new deterministic rate-limit fixture
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested addition of cursor pagination and auth-aware rate limiting that fits the existing repository/DI patterns, though the per-instance uuid limiter key_prefix undermines the distributed limit and the measured 0.73 convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py) rather than by this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 5 changed the GET /tasks response shape from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API change that any consumer built against the session 3 interface would have to adapt to.
Hardcoded JWT_SECRET fallback ('development-secret-change-me') introduced in session 2 was never revisited, leaving a persistent security smell through the end of the story.
Session 2 established created_at DESC as canonical list ordering, but session 5's cursor pagination orders by id DESC — a subtle ordering inconsistency across the two list paths.
Schema bootstrap lives on UserRepository.initialize_database, which creates both users and tasks tables — a functional but confusing layering leak introduced in the session 4 refactor.
Build artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc, todos.db) were committed in almost every session; the agent cleaned them in session 1 but tests recreated them and later commits re-included them.
Rate limiter and Celery broker both default to redis://localhost:6379/0, coupling two unrelated subsystems to the same Redis instance and port.
key_decisions: Session 1 established the baseline discipline: input-validation hardening, timezone-aware timestamps, and idempotent module-level init_db() that made the API robust and testable from the start.

Session 2's JWT auth with per-user task ownership plus a backward-compatible 'legacy' user migration was the pivotal architectural choice — every later session (notifications, pagination, rate limiting) is keyed off that auth seam.
Session 3 decoupled async notifications behind a Celery .delay() seam, dispatching only on a status transition and falling back to username when no email is set — keeping the API unit-testable.

Session 4's repository-pattern extraction (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository + UserRepository) cleanly separated persistence from the Flask app, enabling session 5's pagination to be added at the data layer.
Session 5 added cursor-based pagination and subject-aware rate limiting (JWT user ID when authenticated, IP otherwise), layering cross-cutting concerns onto the existing auth and repository seams.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 tightened the seed with validation and idempotent bootstrap (3 tests); session 2 added a coherent, well-tested auth and ownership feature (4 tests); session 3 integrated Celery notifications through a clean delay() seam with transition-only semantics (6 tests); session 4 was a behavior-preserving refactor that slimmed app.py and pushed SQL into repositories with tests still green; session 5 layered pagination and rate limiting with careful input validation and 9 passing tests. The system moved from a single-file app to a structured app + repositories + celery_config + tasks layout, with test coverage growing in both count and scope at each step. The only flat spots are hygiene issues — a hardcoded secret, id-vs-created_at ordering drift, a breaking list-response change, and committed build artifacts — none of which undermined the overall upward arc.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent greenfield→feature→integration→refactor→cross-cutting arc where each session built deliberately on the prior auth and repository seams, improving structure and test coverage while accruing only minor hygiene and ordering debts.
